'''Upper Umpqua''' is an extinct [[Athabaskan language]] formerly spoken along the south fork of the [[Umpqua River]] in west-central [[Oregon]] by [[Upper Umpqua people|Upper Umpqua]] (Etnemitane) people in the vicinity of modern [[Roseburg, Oregon|Roseburg]]. It has been extinct for at least seventy years and little is known about it other than it belongs to the same ''Oregon Athabaskan'' cluster of [[Pacific Coast Athabaskan languages]] as the [[Tututni language|Lower Rogue River language]], [[Galice language|Upper Rogue River language]] and [[Tolowa language|Chetco-Tolowa]]. 

The most important documentation of Upper Umpqua is the extensive vocabulary obtained by [[Horatio Hale]] in 1841 (published in Hale 1846). [[Melville Jacobs]] and [[John P. Harrington]] were able to collect fragmentary data from the last speakers as late as the 1940s (Golla 2011:70-72). Although known to early explorers and settlers as ''Umpqua,'' the language is now usually called ''Upper Umpqua'' to distinguish it from the unrelated Oregon Coast [[Penutian]] language ''Lower Umpqua'' ([[Siuslaw language|Kuitsh or Siuslaw language]]) that was spoken closer to the coast in the same area.
